source.title: Unveiling m-Sharpness Through the Structure of Stochastic Gradient Noise
source.authors: Hao-Cheng Luo; Mehrtash Harandi; Dinh Q. Phung; Trung Le

record.tranche_reason: The study varies m-SAM micro-batch size and reports test accuracy, directly testing the m-sharpness batch-size effect in a new experiment.
record.gate_note: The study reports test accuracy rather than training error or a train–test gap. Its m-SAM and m-USAM micro-batch sweeps bear on V5; its SGN covariance trace is related to generalization but does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness named in V7. Other optimizer comparisons and label-noise results do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study tests SAM perturbation micro-batch size while keeping the outer update batch fixed, so it does not test V5's large training-batch claim. Its covariance trace is neither magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance nor a measured generalization gap, so it does not test V7. No own results test the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors attribute m-sharpness to implicit stochastic-gradient variance regularization that strengthens as micro-batch size decreases, and propose parallelizable RW-SAM to approximate its generalization benefits. They present theory and empirical associations, rather than a test of V5 or V7 as defined here.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and evaluates SAM micro-batch perturbation variants and proposes RW-SAM; it does not test the original claim's fixed-epoch large outer-batch comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported test accuracy varies with perturbation micro-batch size m; lower m gives higher accuracy across the listed m-SAM and m-USAM results.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, test accuracy rises as SAM micro-batch size decreases: 79.35% at m = 64 to 80.72% at m = 8, versus 78.90% for mini-batch SAM and 78.15% for n-SAM. USAM shows the same micro-batch trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed outer update batch size, smaller micro-batches for SAM or USAM perturbations and perturbed gradients improve held-out accuracy in this setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Converged gradient-covariance trace is 572.39 for SGD, 198.40 for SAM, and 177.79 for RW-SAM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These training methods reach solutions with different stochastic-gradient covariance traces; the comparison does not establish V7's sharpness–generalization-gap relationship.

record.problems: The reported empirical gap evidence is test accuracy rather than train–test error. The m-SAM comparisons vary perturbation micro-batch size rather than outer batch size. The SGN covariance result is a convergence measurement and does not directly establish a relationship with the train–test gap.
record.rows_left_out: Other optimizer test-accuracy comparisons (Tables 1–5 and 9), label-noise results (Table 4), and the poor-minimum escape figures (Figures 1–2) do not measure the behavior named by the tested V5 version. The covariance rows are retained as findings about the claim's subject but do not map to V7.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fixed-random-label fitting alongside natural-label held-out generalization using the same architecture and recipe; label-noise robustness alone does not establish this.
Test error as width increases beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning. The GLUE comparisons use AdamW as their common base optimizer.
Held-out performance across outer training-batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets, and adaptations that reduce the large-batch penalty.
Dropout interventions, small-data failures, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with measured generalization gaps at comparable training loss, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both extracted V5 verdicts. Reporting test accuracy is sufficient for V5's held-out-performance outcome; the decisive mismatch is the batch-size intervention. Throughout the record, SAM, USAM, SGD, and RW-SAM name training algorithms; ResNet-18 is the model.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning recipes.
The study varies SAM perturbation micro-batch size, not the outer batch size; it does not test language models, workload-dependent thresholds, or the listed recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation tolerance and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and retraining.

rows.note: Table 7 reports the m-SAM result separately for each m.

rows.subject: n-SAM
rows.operation_detail: Train with full-batch perturbation n-SAM; report test accuracy.
rows.note: The text describes n-SAM as a contrasting variant; its result is below mini-batch SAM and the m-SAM settings.
rows.check: n-SAM uses the full dataset for its perturbation and a stochastic mini-batch for its outer gradient. It is not full-batch training under V5. Its lower accuracy also points in the same direction as the micro-batch trend, so reversed was misleading.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-100, ResNet-18, m-SAM and m-USAM micro-batch sweep
reader_labels.reason: All reported m-SAM settings exceed mini-batch SAM test accuracy; the m-USAM settings also exceed mini-batch USAM, with smaller gains at m = 64 (R1–R5, R7–R11). The study measures perturbation micro-batch size, not outer batch size.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: n-SAM is below mini-batch SAM in test accuracy, but this comparison does not test the version's fixed-epoch large outer-batch claim (R6).
